reference.source: Dhingra, Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat
clinicalPearls: Tinnitus is the perception of sound in the absence of an external source and is a symptom rather than a disease in itself
It is usefully divided into subjective tinnitus, heard only by the patient, and the much rarer objective tinnitus, which can also be detected by the examiner
Most subjective tinnitus accompanies sensorineural hearing loss from noise exposure, presbycusis, ototoxic drugs or Meniere disease
Pulsatile tinnitus that is synchronous with the heartbeat suggests a vascular cause such as a glomus tumour, an arteriovenous malformation or a dural sinus abnormality and needs vascular imaging
Rhythmic clicking that is not pulse-synchronous may be due to palatal or middle ear muscle myoclonus or a patulous Eustachian tube
Unilateral tinnitus with asymmetrical hearing loss should prompt evaluation for a retrocochlear lesion such as an acoustic neuroma
Aggravating factors such as ototoxic and other implicated medications, caffeine, stress and poor sleep should be reviewed

Because there is often no curative treatment, management centres on treating any underlying cause, hearing aids or sound therapy for masking, and cognitive and habituation-based approaches such as tinnitus retraining therapy
reference.pathophysiology: Subjective tinnitus is thought to arise from aberrant neural activity generated when the cochlea or auditory nerve is damaged; loss of input leads to maladaptive changes and increased spontaneous firing and reorganisation in the central auditory pathways, so the brain perceives sound that is not present. Emotional and attentional networks amplify and sustain the perception, which explains why distress and the loudness of tinnitus are only loosely related. Objective tinnitus, in contrast, has a genuine internal acoustic source: turbulent or pulsatile blood flow in vascular lesions, or repetitive contraction of palatal, tensor tympani or stapedius muscles, generates a real sound transmitted to the ear.
additionalDifferentials: Noise-induced or age-related sensorineural hearing loss
Acoustic neuroma or other retrocochlear lesion
Vascular causes (glomus tumour, arteriovenous malformation, carotid or dural sinus disease)
Palatal or middle ear myoclonus and patulous Eustachian tube
additionalInvestigations: Otoscopy and pure tone audiometry to characterise associated hearing loss
Tympanometry and acoustic reflex testing where middle ear or myoclonic causes are suspected
Tinnitus pitch and loudness matching for assessment and rehabilitation
MRI of the internal auditory meatus for unilateral or asymmetrical tinnitus
CT/MR angiography or venography for pulsatile tinnitus
Blood tests for anaemia, thyroid dysfunction or vascular risk factors where clinically indicated
redFlags: Unilateral tinnitus with asymmetrical hearing loss suggesting a retrocochlear tumour
Pulsatile tinnitus requiring vascular imaging to exclude a treatable vascular lesion
Associated neurological signs, facial numbness or weakness
Sudden hearing loss accompanying the tinnitus, which is an emergency
Tinnitus with severe distress, depression or suicidal ideation needing urgent mental health support
reference.prognosis: Many patients habituate over time and cope well with reassurance, sound enrichment and psychological approaches, and tinnitus linked to a treatable cause may improve when that cause is addressed; however, some individuals have persistent, distressing tinnitus that requires ongoing support.
pitfalls: Missing an acoustic neuroma behind unilateral tinnitus
Failing to image pulsatile tinnitus for a vascular source
Dismissing the symptom without exploring its psychological impact and sleep disturbance
Overlooking ototoxic medication or reversible contributors
Promising a cure rather than framing management around control and habituation
references: Dhingra, Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat
management: Identify and treat any underlying cause, such as fitting hearing aids for sensorineural loss, managing Meniere disease or stopping ototoxic drugs
Investigate and refer red-flag patterns: unilateral or asymmetrical tinnitus for MRI of the internal auditory meatus to exclude an acoustic neuroma, and pulsatile tinnitus for vascular imaging
Offer sound enrichment or masking to reduce the prominence of the tinnitus
Provide psychological therapies such as cognitive behavioural therapy and tinnitus retraining therapy to aid habituation and reduce distress
Give reassurance and education, explaining that tinnitus is a symptom and that most people habituate over time
Treat associated anxiety, depression and insomnia, which amplify and sustain the perception
Consider treatment directed at objective causes, such as intervention for a vascular lesion or management of palatal or middle-ear myoclonus
